title: Two clear liquids can sit unchanged for seconds, then turn blue-black in an instant

cover.alt: A glass beaker of blue-black liquid on a magnetic stirrer, between two empty measuring cylinders labelled A and B.

body: In the **iodine clock reaction**, hydrogen peroxide slowly turns iodide in the mixture into iodine. But thiosulfate, also in the mix, turns each bit of iodine straight back into iodide, so no colour can build up. Only when the thiosulfate is used up does iodine start to collect, and it instantly forms a blue-black complex with starch. The amount of thiosulfate sets the timer: more of it, longer wait. Hans Landolt first described a version of this reaction in 1886.

slides.alt: Two clear solutions are poured together into a beaker on a stirrer with a timer. The mixture stays clear for about twelve seconds, then suddenly turns blue-black all at once.
slides.caption: Two clear solutions go into the beaker at once and the timer starts. For about 12 seconds nothing seems to happen, then the whole beaker turns blue-black.

slides.music: “I Can Feel it Coming” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Does it make the wait shorter or longer?
slides.explanation: Anything that speeds up the slow first step brings the colour sooner. More thiosulfate means more iodine has to be made before any can be left over.

slides.heading: A lesson in reaction speed
slides.text: The iodine clock is a classic way to show chemical kinetics, the study of how fast reactions go. Because the colour appears only when a set amount of iodine has been made, the waiting time measures the speed of the slow first reaction.

slides.question: What makes the sudden blue-black colour?
slides.explanation: Once the thiosulfate has run out, iodine builds up and forms a dark blue complex with the starch in the mixture.
